title: Two minutes in
objective: Administer the 6-minute walk test by protocol on a 30 m course with a pulse oximeter and Borg scale, and report distance and symptoms to the PT
secondaryObjectives: Monitoring vital signs and activity tolerance during a treatment session and responding to abnormal findings

brief.situation: 13:00 in an outpatient pulmonary rehabilitation clinic. You are the physical therapist assistant. Dr. Shah, PT, asked you to run a 6-minute walk test for Mrs. Lindgren, 68, who has pulmonary fibrosis, on the clinic's 30 m hallway course.
handover: Protocol: rest seated 10 minutes; record resting heart rate, SpO2 and Borg dyspnea; walk with a pulse oximeter; standard phrases each minute; she may slow or rest; record distance and symptoms.
The plan's stop rule: SpO2 under 85% on this patient's lung disease, chest pain, severe dyspnea, staggering or pallor: stop, seat her, and tell the PT, who decides about oxygen.
Dr. Shah is in the next room.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time at the pace you choose: study pace (3x) or exam realism (1x). Pause any time.
Each question or measure takes the time on its button. Decide what to collect, what it means for today's session and who needs to know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: Walking with fibrosis, her saturation falls steeply. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.

Seated and rested, her saturation recovers slowly. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.

The authored point where SpO2 falls under 85% with marked breathlessness. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.

The authored point of collapse in the hallway. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.
The PT told within 5 minutes of the stop rule (the plan).
Walk stopped and she is seated within 5 minutes of the stop rule (the plan; the profile's 2-minute stop window is stricter).
A focused assessment or question: about 1 min.
About 10 minutes for the PT to reexamine and decide about oxygen and the plan; finishing the visit as planned about 25 minutes.

Urging her on for the full six minutes after the stop rule: she collapses in this authored course. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.

why.question: Mrs. Lindgren's saturation is under 85% two minutes in. What does that mean for the test, and who decides?

parts.label: What the data show
parts.criteria: Exercise-induced desaturation below the plan's floor with severe dyspnea and dusky lips: a stop rule; the distance and lowest SpO2 at stopping are the result.
parts.modelAnswer: She's desaturating below 85% with severe breathlessness and dusky lips. That's the plan's stop rule; the distance and the lowest saturation are the result to report.

parts.label: What I do and who decides

parts.modelAnswer: I stop the test, sit her down, note the distance, time and lowest saturation, and get Dr. Shah now. Oxygen and the plan are her decisions.

unsafe.headline: Urged on past the rule
unsafe.body: Patients may slow or stop in a 6-minute walk; a stop rule ends it. The distance is never worth a collapse.

scoring.modelReasoning: A 6-minute walk follows its protocol: resting measures, an oximeter throughout, minute checks, chairs ready. In lung disease a saturation below the plan's floor with severe dyspnea is a stop rule. The PTA stops the test, seats her, records the distance, time and lowest SpO2, and tells the PT now; oxygen and the plan are the PT's decisions.

deQ.ask: While you check the minute: in this patient's lung disease, which SpO2 is a stop criterion?

choices.label: SpO2 is not a stop criterion

deQ.explain: Stop criteria include SpO2 under 90% or a 4% drop for acute coronary syndrome, and under 85% in lung disease.
